video.title: Why Pros Hit So Far Away

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and cues, such as holding a cone in the non-hitting hand and performing a lunge drill without taking steps to find the optimal hitting slot.

problem.title_as_question: Why do professional players hit the forehand so far away from their body?
problem.definition: Players habitually set up too close to the ball and get jammed at contact, preventing proper trunk rotation, forward elbow drive, and weight transfer.
problem.target_player: Players who intuitively crowd the ball or use a pushing hitting lane

symptoms.description: The player feels jammed at contact and awkward having to lean back and push the ball.
The hitting arm collapses into a chicken wing or gets stuck behind the rotating trunk.
The swing falls off to the left instead of the body driving through the court.
The player over-reaches into a butt-back, racket-forward posture when trying too hard to create space.

causes.statement: Players intuitively revert to an old jammed contact point and pushing hitting lane close to their body.
The non-hitting arm is left dangling or pulled in rather than extended across the body to gauge lateral spacing and stabilize trunk balance.
Weight remains centered back on the heels during loading, causing the drive to fall back to the left instead of through the court.
The player sets up without sufficient forward depth space to accommodate arm clearance during trunk rotation.

angles.summary: The correct hitting slot feels comically far off to the right compared to the habitual jammed pushing contact point.
Hitting with the non-hitting arm dangling versus pushed out demonstrates that an inactive arm degrades balance, trunk coordination, and spacing.
Sufficient lateral spacing enables the elbow to drive forward in the same direction the torso faces along a pressing vector.
Vertical spacing requires swinging on a gentle upward diagonal with the hand rolling through the ball rather than dive-bombing from high preparation.
Aggressive footwork should not mean running directly into the ball and jamming the forward depth space needed for arm penetration.

solutions.summary: Push your non-hitting arm across your body in preparation to act as a balance and spacing cue.
Hold an object like a cone in your non-hitting hand during preparation to intuitively keep the arm extended and activate spatial awareness.
solutions.external_goal: Hold a cone in your non-hitting hand

solutions.summary: Progress from holding a cone to holding a 2.5-pound weight in the non-hitting hand to increase visceral stability feedback on the non-hitting side.
solutions.external_goal: Hold a 2.5 lb weight in your non-hitting hand

solutions.summary: Do the lunge drill by freezing your feet and lunging to hit balls fed comically far to your right, learning to rotate and release cleanly without getting jammed.
solutions.external_goal: Hit balls fed comically far away without taking extra steps

solutions.summary: Leave several extra inches of depth in front of you when planning to lean in so your trunk movement does not crowd the arm's forward path.
